newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call money ends higher, gilts steady.
newsitem.headline: Indian call money ends higher, gilts steady.

text.p: Indian call money ended Thursday in the 10.5-11.0 percent range on late demand from a few banks after opening at 4.5-5.0 percent range, dealers said.
They said rates firmed up on demand in late trade after being range-bound in a 5.75-6.25 band for most of the day.
"There seem to be two factors behind the rise in rates," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "One is outflow on account of tax payments by corporates."
He said advance taxes paid by corporates earlier this month, estimated to be between 40 and 50 billion rupees, had started flowing out of banks.
"It appears that the outflows may have hit some lenders, reducing the supply of funds in the market," he said. "This pushed rates up."

The second factor could be that some banks had left positions uncovered before the reporting day, anticipating lower call rates, he said. Banks report their positions to the Reserve Bank of India on Friday.

"Usually, rates come down on the eve of the reporting Friday," he said. "Some banks may have postponed their borrowings, hoping to borrow at lower rates. When this did not happen, there was panic borrowing, pushing up rates."

Dealers said yields on government securities moved up marginally in dull trade. The 13.50 percent 1998 government of India stock traded on Thursday at a yield of 12.32 percent against its last traded 12.28 percent, they said.
The 14 percent 2006 stock was steady at 13.73 percent while treasury bills maturing on January 29, 1997 yielded eight percent against last trade of 7.25 percent, they said.
Dealers said there were no trades in commercial paper or certificates of deposit.
